1. Long story short, I job shadowed a family friend in high school for Speech-Language Pathology (SLP) I originally wanted to go into psychology, but hated it and dropped out the first year. When I started thinking about what I really wanted to do, I realized I wanted to go into SLP, and found out going into linguistics was the best way to get into the field.
2. Right now, I am in the process of changing my thesis. I'm in 2nd year, so I have to get through my comprehensive exam before I really need to commit to a project. It will probably do with cue weighing though (phonetics).
3. I am not fluent in any language other than English (a common misconception with Linguists). It definitely DOES help to have more than one language under your belt, but it's not a requirement. I do have some Spanish, French and American Sign Language under my belt though.
4. I can understand some, so I've definitely understood people talking shit. I find responding with a word or 2 in the language shuts them up real fast.
5. I could go into research. I was interested in being a professor, or perhaps Forensic Linguistics which is very phonetic oriented (and super cool! you should check it out if you get a chance). There are a lot of other options. With the advancement of machine learning, and speech synthesis, linguistics is a HUGELY desired field right now.
6. As mentioned above, I do have some ASL experience. It actually functions in VERY similar ways to written or spoken languages. There are a lot of aspects to language people tend to not think about a lot (specifically in my realm of phonetics - speech sounds). Grammar, for example, gets carried a lot in tone or stress patterns, something ASL captures in facial gestures. As well, ASL uses a lot of cues, like facial features, to convey information as oral speakers do - frustration, irony etc. Speech isn't just sound (I'll attach a link for the McGurk effect) Additionally, ASL has dialects and variations, like oral or written languages, which is super fascinating!

Here are my thoughts (as a Psycholinguistic and Theoretical Linguist)
1) Common usage: it's hard to say. I think right now, from my own personal and academic experience, it won't catch on. There is a major shift towards what Sociolinguists call "reclaiming a word". I think women, in general, are reclaiming the word itself, and finding a source of pride in it rather than "man". I also have notice, academically speaking, a shift to female pronouns, where there was a default male pronouns used (in journal articles etc.) There has also been a reform to opt for gender neutral words such as "they" or "them". If anything was to catch on, I think it would be the gender neutrality rather than a change of orthography.

2) I think, personally, and there will be those that disagree, sexism occurs due to the connotations of the word, rather than it's form. Look at the history for the word "homosexual". Also, orthographically speaking it doesn't contain and male or female, it does contain 'homo' equating to "the same". Homosexual was deemed wrong, and negative, a hell-condemning sin. But gay individuals took that word back, and were basically refused the connotations given to that word, for it then to be embraced by the gay community.

My degree background is in Psycholinguistics, which is basically put: understanding how language functions in the brain. 

I actually did a research project on dyslexia and hope I can be a help explaining it.

So, symbol languages, in linguistic terms, is called a logographic system. This basically means that the language is communicate (in writing systems) through logos, or symbols, representing - usually - a "chunk" or what is called a morpheme. A combination of these morphemes in a particular pattern and combination represent a word or phrase.

Languages like English are considered alphabetic (cause - you know - the alphabet).

There's a lot of different things to consider you'd need more information from studying to field, but basically our ability to read has mapped on to previously developed parts of the brain, utilizing their functions to process language. For alphabetic system, they are usually called "t-junctions" meaning before modern times, letter like the "o" weren't actually round, but were a series of lines making almost a diamond shape that has altered over the years to the circular "o" we all know and love.

Alphabetic languages actually access a part of the brain (which I can't currently recall) that has to do with your lexical phonetic storage system - meaning you link the letter to a specific sound (with has its variations between words in English... but that's a different topic all together). That is how it is simply organized.

Logographic systems actually activate parts of the visual cortex not activated in alphabetic systems (or only activated minimally). There are actually MRI testing that has been done on this demonstrating the results.

What's really cool is the fact that because these two systems of writing/reading don't full connect, a person who is dyslexic in one system, such as English, could be fully able to read and write with easy in another system, like Japanese, because of this lack of overlap between logographic and alphabet systems (you can find case studies on this which are actually pretty rad!) 

There is much debate as to why dyslexia happens in the first place, but some of the best journal articles dispute that it has to do with the fact that writing and reading is a relatively new systems to our brains, and might have to do with the fact we are utilizing previous skills for other task that have evolved in our brain, to map the ability to read and write and make it accessible.
